cards.front: What is the structure of the Earth?
cards.back: Inner core (solid iron/nickel), Outer core (liquid), Mantle (semi-molten rock), Crust (solid rock).

cards.front: What are tectonic plates?
cards.back: Large slabs of crust and upper mantle (lithosphere) that move on the asthenosphere.

cards.front: What causes plate movement?
cards.back: Convection currents in the mantle. Heat from core causes magma to rise, cool, sink - circular motion drags plates.

cards.front: Name the 3 types of plate boundaries.
cards.back: Constructive (divergent), Destructive (convergent), Conservative (transform).

cards.front: What happens at a constructive plate boundary?
cards.back: Plates move apart. Magma rises, cools, forms new crust. Creates mid-ocean ridges, shield volcanoes, gentle earthquakes.

cards.front: What happens at a destructive plate boundary (oceanic-continental)?
cards.back: Denser oceanic plate subducts under continental. Deep ocean trench, fold mountains, composite volcanoes, violent earthquakes.

cards.front: What happens at a destructive plate boundary (continental-continental)?
cards.back: Neither subducts easily. Both buckle upwards forming high fold mountains (e.g., Himalayas). Shallow earthquakes, no volcanoes.

cards.front: What happens at a conservative plate boundary?
cards.back: Plates slide past each other. No crust created/destroyed. Shallow earthquakes, no volcanoes. E.g., San Andreas Fault.

cards.front: What are the two types of volcanoes at plate boundaries?
cards.back: Shield volcanoes (constructive, runny lava, gentle slopes) and Composite/Strato volcanoes (destructive, viscous lava, steep sides, explosive).

cards.front: What is the Richter scale?
cards.back: Logarithmic scale measuring earthquake magnitude. Each whole number = 10x amplitude, ~31.6x energy release.

cards.front: What is the Mercalli scale?
cards.back: Measures earthquake intensity based on observed damage/effects (I-XII). Subjective, varies by location.

cards.front: Primary effects of earthquakes:
cards.back: Ground shaking, ground rupture, liquefaction, landslides, tsunamis (if underwater).

cards.front: Secondary effects of earthquakes:
cards.back: Fires (gas leaks), disease (water contamination), homelessness, economic disruption, aftershocks.

cards.front: Immediate responses to earthquakes:
cards.back: Search & rescue, emergency aid (food/water/shelter), medical treatment, restoring utilities, evacuation.

cards.front: Long-term responses to earthquakes:
cards.back: Rebuilding infrastructure, improving building codes, early warning systems, education/drills, economic recovery.

cards.front: Why do people live in tectonically active areas?
cards.back: Fertile volcanic soils, geothermal energy, tourism, mineral resources, cultural/historical ties, lack of alternatives.

cards.front: How can volcanic eruptions be monitored/predicted?
cards.back: Seismometers (earthquakes), tiltmeters/GPS (ground deformation), gas emissions (SO₂), thermal imaging, satellite monitoring.

cards.front: How can earthquake impacts be reduced?
cards.back: Building design (base isolation, cross-bracing), land-use zoning, early warning systems, emergency planning, education.

cards.front: Compare effects of earthquakes in HIC vs LIC (e.g., Japan 2011 vs Haiti 2010).
cards.back: HIC: Better buildings, warning systems, emergency services, insurance, faster recovery. LIC: Poor construction, no warning, limited aid, slow recovery, higher death toll.

cards.front: What is a supervolcano? Example?
cards.back: Erupts >1,000 km³ material. Global climate impact (volcanic winter). Yellowstone (USA), Toba (Indonesia). Rare but catastrophic.
